meta.title: FlyUp — "Pilot Profile" Situational Judgment Test
meta.inspiredBy: TD12 (not a reproduction of the proprietary instrument)
meta.disclaimer: Training tool inspired by the TD12 format. It has no clinical diagnostic value and is not a reproduction of an existing proprietary test.

items.situation: Two technical solutions exist for a failure: one well known but longer, the other faster but less mastered.

options.text: You hesitate for a long time without deciding, delaying necessary action.
You choose the well-mastered solution even if it takes longer.
You choose the fast solution if the documentation clearly validates it.
You choose the fast solution because time is pressing.

items.situation: A strong crosswind makes the landing borderline relative to the aircraft's limits.

options.text: You attempt the landing while staying ready to go around if needed.
You attempt the landing without reassessing the limits on final approach.
You continue without paying particular attention to the wind parameter.
You precisely assess the limits and go around or divert if they are exceeded.

items.situation: You notice a minor anomaly during the pre-flight walkaround.

options.text: You decide on your own that it's not serious and depart without reporting it.
You don't mention it to anyone.
You report it and wait for resolution before departure if necessary.
You note it for reporting after the flight.

items.situation: A cabin crew member reports a doubt about whether a door is properly closed.

options.text: You request a check but continue other tasks in parallel.
You have it checked immediately and wait for confirmation before proceeding.
You ignore the remark since it doesn't come from the flight deck.
You tell them it's probably nothing, without further verification.

items.situation: An internal client (another company department) pressures you on an operational decision.

options.text: You calmly explain the operational constraints and maintain your decision if justified.
You partially give in to ease the tension.
You dig in and refuse any dialogue.
You give in entirely to avoid conflict.

items.situation: A discrepancy appears between the weather forecast and what you actually observe in flight.

options.text: You continue according to the original forecast without factoring in the observation.
You hesitate for a long time between the two sources without deciding.
You ignore the discrepancy, since forecasts are generally reliable.
You trust your direct observation and adjust your decision accordingly.

items.situation: You feel a drop in concentration during a repetitive monitoring task in cruise.

options.text: You continue without changing anything, the situation isn't critical.
You wait for the fatigue to pass on its own.
You consciously vary your monitoring activity and involve your crew.
You let your attention lapse without realizing it.

items.situation: You notice repeated mistakes on your part toward the end of duty.

options.text: You carry on as normal, they're minor mistakes in your view.
You try harder on your own without reporting it.
You pay no attention to it.
You tell your crew and reinforce cross-checking.

items.situation: You made a minor mistake that had no visible consequence.

options.text: You deliberately conceal it to avoid any consequence for yourself.
You report it for review, even without a visible consequence.
You note it for yourself without officially reporting it.
You don't report it, judging it unimportant.

items.situation: You need to motivate a tired crew for the final leg of a difficult day.

options.text: You downplay the fatigue so as not to demotivate the crew further.
You pile on the pressure without acknowledging the difficulty experienced.
You acknowledge the shared fatigue while refocusing on the rigor needed through to the end.
You let everyone manage their own motivation individually.

items.situation: An internal quality audit flags a minor deviation in your practice.

options.text: You take the remark into account and adjust your practice accordingly.
You note the remark without immediately changing your practice.
You dispute the remark without really analyzing it.
You ignore it, assuming it doesn't really concern you.

items.situation: Your first officer quietly mentions a doubt about the safety altitude, without pressing the point.

options.text: You pay no attention, assuming they would have insisted if it were important.
You ask them to state it clearly as soon as possible, without interrupting the current maneuver.
You immediately ask for clarification and verify the point together before continuing.
You note the information, telling yourself you'll come back to it later.

items.situation: A decision must be made quickly but the crew is divided on the course of action.

options.text: You decide without listening to opinions, for lack of time.
You briefly listen to the views then decide clearly, explaining why.
You let the debate continue without deciding, risking wasted time.
You ask someone else to decide in your place.

items.situation: An important passenger insists on preferential treatment that bends safety rules.

options.text: You grant a small allowance so as not to upset the passenger.
You fully give in to their request.
You refuse any exception to the safety rules, regardless of the passenger's status.
You politely but firmly explain that you cannot deviate from the rule.

items.situation: During the pre-flight briefing, you have an important technical point to convey but the crew seems in a hurry.

options.text: You summarize the point in one quick sentence and offer to revisit it in flight if needed.
You postpone the point to avoid delaying departure.
You drop the point, assuming it's probably not essential.
You take the time needed to convey the key point despite the time pressure.

items.situation: There is personal tension with a colleague you have to fly with.

options.text: You limit exchanges to the strict minimum without resolving the tension.
You set the personal disagreement aside and adopt a strictly professional stance.
You ask to be replaced without looking for another solution.
You let the tension affect in-flight communication.

items.situation: You must choose between two possible procedures for a failure, without absolute certainty about the best option.

options.text: You let your first officer decide alone so as not to make a mistake.
You quickly choose the option that seems simplest to execute.
You wait until you have all the information before deciding, even if it takes time.
You choose the safest option based on the available information and consult if possible.

items.situation: You notice your first officer seems drowsy during cruise.

options.text: You don't notice the situation.
You let it be, without intervening, it's not your place.
You start a conversation and propose an adapted task split.
You take on more tasks yourself without telling them.

items.situation: The airline offers you a duty extension at the end of the day.

options.text: You objectively assess your fatigue level before accepting or declining.
You systematically accept so as not to disrupt the schedule.
You systematically decline on principle, without assessing your real state.
You decide on a whim, depending on your mood at the moment.

items.situation: A minor alarm triggers during a stable cruise phase.

options.text: You ignore the alarm if it doesn't seem serious.
You methodically analyze the situation before acting, following the appropriate procedure.
You act quickly based on your first impression.
You wait to see if the alarm recurs before acting.

items.situation: A collective crew decision differs from the personal opinion you expressed beforehand.

options.text: You carry it out half-heartedly, keeping your reservations to yourself.
You keep arguing for your position instead of executing the decision made.
You support the collective decision while staying alert during its execution.
You quietly undermine the execution of the decision.

items.situation: A duty involves reduced rest before a sensitive early-morning flight.

options.text: You organize your rest as a priority to be fit for duty.
You count on coffee and preparation before the flight to compensate.
You accept personal activities that further reduce your rest.
You change nothing about your sleep habits.

items.situation: You're alone to perform a technical check normally done by two people.

options.text: You wait for a second checker to be available as required by the procedure.
You perform the check alone with extra care.
You skip the check due to unavailability.
You perform the check alone without any particular precaution.

items.situation: A passenger has a serious medical emergency in flight.

options.text: You let the cabin crew handle the situation alone.
You wait for a doctor on board's opinion before any decision.
You continue to the original destination while monitoring the situation.
You assess the need for a medical diversion with the crew and decide quickly.

items.situation: You feel tired at the start of the last leg of a long day.

options.text: You completely ignore your state, it's not a big deal in your view.
You carry on as normal without mentioning it, thinking it will pass.
You downplay your fatigue so as not to delay the flight.
You inform your crew and increase your vigilance on key points.

items.situation: A checklist is taking longer than expected and the flight is running late.

options.text: You complete the checklist in full despite the schedule pressure.
You skip some points you consider secondary to save time.
You read it faster without skipping any steps.
You run through the checklist from memory without the paper support.

items.situation: Your line manager asks you to justify a decision you made alone in flight.

options.text: You stay vague about your reasoning.
You clearly explain your reasoning and the factors that drove it.
You shift the responsibility onto another crew member.
You downplay your role in the decision to avoid scrutiny.

items.situation: Smoke appears in the cabin during the flight.

options.text: You monitor the situation for a few minutes before deciding on a diversion.
You apply the smoke/fire procedure and consider a diversion without delay.
You wait for instructions from the cabin before acting.
You continue to the planned destination if the smoke seems to be clearing.

items.situation: An unexpected event temporarily unsettles your crew.

options.text: You calmly take back the initiative, structure priorities and reassure the crew.
You wait for the situation to settle on its own before intervening.
You let everyone react individually without coordination.
You show your own worry without structuring a response.

items.situation: The procedure requires a cross-check you consider redundant in this specific case.

options.text: You skip it, judging it useless in this particular case.
You perform it quickly, somewhat less thoroughly than usual.
You ask your first officer to do it in your place without checking.
You perform it anyway, since the procedure exists for a reason.

items.situation: You're pressed for time and an administrative step before the flight seems superfluous.

options.text: You complete it in full despite the time constraint.
You postpone it until after the flight.
You complete a simplified but substantively complete version of it.
You don't complete it at all.

items.situation: The captain makes a decision that seems risky to you.

options.text: You carry out the decision without reacting, even in deep disagreement.
You stay silent, assuming they have good reasons.
You make a cautious remark without pressing further.
You clearly state your disagreement and your reasons, assertively.

items.situation: Important information needs to be passed to the cabin crew just before landing.

options.text: You pass it on quickly without asking for confirmation of receipt.
You don't pass it on, judging it not to be a priority.
You pass it on only if time allows.
You communicate it clearly and confirm it has been received.

items.situation: You must choose between saving time by taking a slight risk or strictly respecting the planned safety margin.

options.text: You slightly reduce the margin while staying within strict regulatory limits.
You systematically take the fastest option.
You take the risk if the probability of a problem seems low to you.
You respect the safety margin even if it costs time.

items.situation: An emergency occurs while you're tired at the end of a duty period.

options.text: You handle it alone so as not to overload an equally tired crew.
You rigorously apply the procedure while actively involving your crew.
You deliberately slow down your decision-making out of excessive caution.
You downplay the situation, hoping it resolves itself.

items.situation: A junior first officer makes a relevant remark about your own flying.

options.text: You downplay the remark due to their lack of experience.
You dismiss it because it comes from a junior first officer.
You politely accept the remark without really taking it into account.
You listen carefully and take it into account if it's justified.

items.situation: You notice your captain seems tired and less responsive than usual.

options.text: You talk to them directly and suggest adjusting the task split.
You quietly compensate without telling them.
You discuss it with other colleagues rather than with them.
You say nothing out of respect for the hierarchy.

items.situation: You realize your food and water intake has been insufficient during a long flying day.

options.text: You correct it as soon as possible and factor it into your vigilance.
You wait until the end of duty to address it.
You don't think about it at all.
You carry on without giving it much thought.

items.situation: A partial double electrical failure reduces the available systems.

options.text: You let the system stabilize on its own before intervening.
You prioritize essential tasks according to the procedure and manage workload with your crew.
You focus on a single system while neglecting the priorities.
You try to restore all systems at once as fast as possible.

items.situation: You need to relay bad operational news (delay, diversion) to the passengers.

options.text: You give minimal information while waiting to learn more.
You delay the announcement, hoping the situation resolves itself.
You let the cabin crew handle the communication without stepping in.
You communicate the information clearly, honestly and reassuringly.

items.situation: An instructor asks you to apply a different method than the one you consider safest.

options.text: You apply their method without expressing your disagreement.
You apply your own method without informing them.
You flatly refuse without discussion.
You explain your point of view while remaining open to their explanations.

items.situation: You must decide on a point of no return (continue or abort the takeoff/approach) within a very short window.

options.text: You follow your gut feeling without reference to the prepared criterion.
You quickly assess the available elements before deciding.
You wait for an additional signal before deciding, risking passing the decision point.
You apply the decision criterion prepared in advance, without hesitation.

items.situation: Your crew doubts the relevance of a decision you just made.

options.text: You ignore the doubt expressed by the crew.
You reverse your decision purely to avoid the doubt expressed.
You explain your reasoning to reassure them and win their support.
You impose the decision without explanation.

items.situation: A new procedure has just been published but you're not yet fully comfortable with it.

options.text: You improvise your own version of the procedure.
You take the time to review it before applying it and ask for advice if needed.
You keep applying the old procedure out of habit.
You apply it directly, referring to the reference material if a doubt arises.

items.situation: You need to evacuate the aircraft on the ground following an alert.

options.text: You order the evacuation immediately per procedure without unnecessary delay.
You take time to confirm the severity before deciding.
You wait for instructions from ground services before acting.
You delay the evacuation to avoid panicking the passengers.

items.situation: A storm forms along the planned track shortly before the aircraft's expected passage.

options.text: You keep the original track, hoping the storm moves away.
You cross the area while simply reducing speed.
You plan a sufficiently wide deviation while anticipating how it will develop.
You adjust the track at the last moment based on what you observe.

items.situation: An experienced colleague suggests a shortcut not covered by the official procedure.

options.text: You systematically follow shortcuts suggested by your colleagues.
You follow the shortcut because the person is experienced.
You politely decline and follow the official procedure.
You accept if the shortcut seems logical to you, without further verification.

items.situation: Your first officer stays silent during a critical phase although they usually call out parameters.

options.text: You carry on as normal, assuming they're handling it.
You ask them directly to understand their silence and check on their state.
You call out the parameters yourself in their place without asking why.
You say nothing, it isn't your concern.

items.situation: An engine failure occurs shortly after takeoff.

options.text: You immediately apply the memorized procedure, then the associated checklist.
You wait for your first officer's confirmation before any action.
You take a few seconds to properly identify the issue before acting.
You improvise a response without referring to the known procedure.

items.situation: You disagree with a company instruction regarding an operational procedure.

options.text: You apply the instruction without ever voicing your opinion.
You quietly bypass the instruction based on your own judgment.
You openly refuse to apply the instruction without formal explanation.
You apply the instruction while escalating your disagreement through the proper channels.

items.situation: An ambiguous situation allows for either a favorable or unfavorable interpretation of your responsibility.

options.text: You present the facts from the most favorable angle for you, without distorting them.
You report the facts objectively, without trying to steer the interpretation.
You alter the facts to clear yourself.
You omit certain awkward details in your report.

items.situation: An incident affects your crew's morale during a long flying day.

options.text: You let morale drop without intervening.
You ignore the human aspect and focus only on the technical tasks.
You acknowledge the difficulty, remotivate the team and refocus on priorities.
You downplay the incident without discussing it again with the team.

items.situation: An engine fire is confirmed by several indications.

options.text: You apply the memorized extinguishing procedure without delay.
You double-check the indications a second time before acting.
You wait until you're on the ground to deal with the problem.
You reduce power on the engine while waiting for other signs.

items.situation: An air traffic controller gives you an instruction you consider unsuited to the situation.

options.text: You don't carry out the instruction without informing the controller.
You carry out the instruction without comment while staying alert.
You politely voice your concern and suggest an alternative.
You firmly dispute the instruction without proposing an alternative.

items.situation: You lose radio communication in controlled airspace.

options.text: You continue as normal, waiting for communication to return.
You try several frequencies before considering a specific procedure.
You change your route without following any defined procedure.
You apply the planned lost-communication (NORDO) procedure.

items.situation: An experienced captain dismisses a safety remark you made.

options.text: You stay silent to avoid creating tension.
You act on your own without bringing it up with them again.
You drop it after one attempt.
You restate your remark more firmly, explaining the safety stakes.

items.situation: A shorter than usual runway is offered for landing due to works.

options.text: You systematically refuse any unusual runway without assessment.
You recalculate the landing performance before accepting the proposed runway.
You accept without a specific check, since the runway is certified.
You accept the runway based on your general experience.

items.situation: An incident involving you could, if reported, affect your professional evaluation.

options.text: You don't report it if you think you can avoid it without consequence.
You report it in full despite the possible consequences for you.
You actively conceal it.
You report it in a downplayed way to limit the impact.

items.situation: You must quickly decide whether or not to interrupt an ongoing maneuver due to a doubt.

options.text: You interrupt the maneuver as a precaution until the doubt is clarified.
You continue because interrupting seems riskier than useful.
You continue while staying ready to interrupt if the doubt is confirmed.
You continue without reassessing, the doubt seeming minor.

items.situation: A low cloud ceiling complicates a visual approach that was initially planned.

options.text: You continue the visual approach hoping for an improvement.
You continue without reassessing which type of approach is best suited.
You try to maintain visual references for as long as possible.
You switch to an appropriate instrument procedure without hesitation.

items.situation: Two members of your crew are in open conflict during preparation.

options.text: You ignore the conflict as long as it doesn't directly affect the flight.
You take one person's side without trying to ease the situation.
You let the two people sort out their differences on their own.
You step in to refocus the team on the mission and ease the tension.

items.situation: A flying day turns out longer than planned due to a significant delay.

options.text: You carry on without reassessing, since the original plan was approved.
You let the airline decide alone without giving your opinion.
You assess the impact on fatigue with your crew and adjust if needed.
You push to complete the planned schedule no matter what.

items.situation: A regulatory document on board recently expired.

options.text: You report it and take the necessary steps to regularize it before the flight.
You don't check that kind of document out of habit.
You ask someone else to take care of it without confirming it's done.
You fly, planning to regularize it after the flight.

items.situation: You need to assign extra tasks following an operational disruption.

options.text: You let everyone choose freely without coordination.
You take on all the extra tasks yourself.
You clearly assign the tasks based on each person's skills and workload.
You assign the tasks randomly without particular consideration.

items.situation: You need to correct a colleague on inappropriate behavior in flight.

options.text: You wait until the end of the flight to raise it, once things are calm.
You discuss it with other colleagues rather than with the person concerned.
You raise the issue directly, factually and respectfully.
You avoid raising the issue so as not to create awkwardness.

items.situation: Icing builds up faster than expected in flight.

options.text: You carry on as normal, hoping to quickly exit the area.
You immediately apply the appropriate anti-icing procedure and reassess the route if needed.
You ignore the phenomenon if it doesn't yet seem significant.
You monitor how it develops before acting.

items.situation: A technical disagreement arises with your first officer during the flight.

options.text: You avoid the subject so as not to inflame the situation.
You leave the disagreement unresolved and each act on your own.
You calmly lay out each person's arguments and look for a fact-based solution.
You impose your view as captain without discussion.

items.situation: A passenger becomes aggressive toward the cabin crew.

options.text: You downplay the incident to avoid making the situation worse.
You let the cabin crew handle it alone without intervening.
You avoid getting directly involved.
You firmly back the cabin crew and apply the procedure planned for this type of situation.

items.situation: A junior crew member lacks confidence in a technical task.

options.text: You do the task in their place to save time.
You criticize them for their lack of confidence.
You let them figure it out alone without support.
You guide them step by step while progressively giving them more responsibility.

items.situation: A decompression occurs at altitude.

options.text: You wait for confirmation from the cabin crew before acting.
You first assess the severity before deciding on a descent.
You continue the flight while monitoring the cabin pressure trend.
You immediately don the masks and initiate an emergency descent per procedure.

items.situation: You discover that a colleague altered a report to avoid a remark.

options.text: You also cover up the information so as not to harm your colleague.
You encourage them to officially correct the report and report it if necessary.
You say nothing, it's not your problem.
You talk to them privately without making an official report.

items.situation: You receive criticism from a superior that you consider unfair.

options.text: You strongly dispute it without arguing on the substance.
You calmly present your point of view with factual elements.
You keep your disagreement to yourself and build resentment.
You accept the criticism without reacting, even in disagreement.

items.situation: The remaining fuel becomes tighter than planned due to an unexpected delay.

options.text: You precisely recalculate the endurance and consider an early diversion if needed.
You closely monitor consumption while continuing to the planned destination.
You continue as normal without a specific recalculation.
You wait until the last minute to assess the fuel situation.

items.situation: The captain asks you to speed up a safety procedure to make up for lost time.

options.text: You comply without discussion, even though it feels risky to you.
You speed up slightly without omitting any essential step.
You skip steps to meet the request.
You refuse to compromise safety and clearly explain why.

items.situation: After a minor in-flight incident, a debrief with the crew is suggested but time is tight.

options.text: You give a quick verbal recap with no particular structure.
You postpone the debrief to another occasion.
You take a few minutes for a structured debrief despite the limited time.
You skip the debrief entirely since the incident was minor.

items.situation: You notice a discrepancy between what you understood and what the controller seems to have said.

options.text: You apply your first understanding without checking.
You wait for the controller to speak again to clarify on their own.
You immediately ask for confirmation by reading back the instruction.
You apply what you think you understood while staying alert for a correction.

items.situation: You take over from a captain in a situation that is already underway.

options.text: You wait a long time before actually taking on the responsibility.
You ask for a clear situation report before taking over the controls.
You immediately take the controls without a clear handover.
You leave it ambiguous as to who is actually flying.

items.situation: You must give critical feedback to a colleague more experienced than you.

options.text: You phrase your feedback factually, respectfully and directly.
You discuss it with others rather than with them directly.
You avoid raising the subject directly.
You phrase the feedback very softly to avoid any discomfort.

items.situation: Strong commercial pressure is applied to shorten preparation time before a technical flight.

options.text: You reduce the preparation to meet the pressure.
You streamline the preparation time without skipping an essential step.
You remove preparation steps deemed secondary.
You maintain the preparation time required for safety.

items.situation: The weather deteriorates rapidly on approach to your destination.

options.text: You follow air traffic control's decision without any personal assessment.
You wait until the last minute to decide on a diversion.
You assess the alternatives (divert, hold) before the safety margin shrinks further.
You continue the approach hoping the weather improves.

items.situation: A new first officer hesitates to speak up even though they've spotted an anomaly.

options.text: You carry on without prompting them, waiting for them to dare speak.
You don't notice their hesitation and carry on.
You explicitly encourage them to speak and value their observation.
You ask what they noticed once the critical phase is over.

items.situation: You must decide whether you're fit to fly a duty after a short night's sleep.

options.text: You go on the flight thinking you can manage despite the fatigue.
You don't even ask yourself the question.
You honestly assess your state and report unfitness if necessary.
You downplay your state so as not to disrupt the schedule.

items.situation: The landing gear doesn't confirm it's down via the usual indicator lights.

options.text: You land normally, hoping the gear is indeed down.
You apply the alternate verification procedure before any decision.
You attempt another extension cycle without consulting the procedure.
You wait for the tower's opinion without checking on board.

items.situation: Significant jet lag disrupts your sleep before a duty period.

options.text: You adjust your rest and report excessive fatigue before the flight if necessary.
You fly, hoping the fatigue will fade during the flight.
You compensate with coffee and fly as normal.
You change nothing about your habits.

items.situation: Visibility drops sharply during an approach phase.

options.text: You continue without reassessing the applicable minima.
You reassess the feasibility of the approach against the minima and decide accordingly.
You continue relying solely on your personal experience.
You continue the approach while staying very attentive to visual references.

items.situation: A team member suggests an idea different from yours to solve a problem.

options.text: You seriously evaluate the suggestion before deciding whether to adopt it.
You don't react to the suggestion at all.
You systematically adopt it without evaluating it, just to value the initiative.
You dismiss it quickly because it differs from your initial idea.

items.situation: A technical parameter is slightly out of range but no alarm is associated with it.

options.text: You monitor its evolution while continuing the mission.
You ignore the parameter, it's not your role to analyze it.
You investigate the cause before continuing normally.
You carry on without paying attention, reassured by the absence of an alarm.

items.situation: The airline insists on operating the flight despite an unresolved minor technical doubt.

options.text: You give in to the pressure to avoid a conflict with the airline.
You hold your safety position and refuse to depart until the doubt is resolved.
You agree to depart while increasing your monitoring of the doubtful item.
You depart without reassessing the technical issue in question.

items.situation: Severe, unexpected turbulence occurs during cruise.

options.text: You reduce speed per procedure and immediately secure the cabin.
You speed up to get out of the turbulent area faster.
You wait for the turbulence to pass before adjusting anything.
You continue without any configuration change.

items.situation: You're asked to overlook a slight regulatory breach to save time.

options.text: You firmly refuse and comply with the regulation.
You voice your discomfort but let it slide this one time.
You start proposing this kind of arrangement yourself in the future.
You accept if the breach seems genuinely minor to you.

items.situation: A commercial instruction is in direct tension with a safety instruction.

options.text: You look for a compromise that preserves safety as the priority.
You systematically prioritize safety over the commercial instruction.
You prioritize the commercial instruction to avoid complications.
You try to satisfy both instructions even if it reduces the safety margin.

items.situation: An exceptional situation requires a quick reorganization of roles on board.

options.text: You keep the usual organization even though it no longer fits.
You let everyone guess their role amid the urgency.
You take on all the roles yourself.
You clearly redefine who does what and check everyone has understood.

items.situation: A standard procedure seems poorly suited to the current situation.

options.text: You do neither the procedure nor an alternative.
You ignore it entirely because you believe you have a better solution.
You follow the procedure while flagging your observation for later review.
You slightly adapt the procedure based on your personal experience.

items.situation: You notice that you and your first officer are interpreting an ATC clearance differently.

options.text: You each continue on your own without coordinating.
You stop the action and clarify together before continuing.
You let your first officer proceed without voicing your disagreement.
You follow your own interpretation while telling your first officer of your choice.

items.situation: A cabin crew member openly challenges one of your decisions in front of the passengers.

options.text: You give in immediately to avoid a scene in front of the passengers.
You completely ignore the public remark.
You stay calm, defer the discussion to private and maintain your decision if justified.
You respond firmly on the spot to close the matter quickly.

items.situation: Conflicting information arrives from two different sources (ATC and onboard system).

options.text: You cross-check the information and ask for confirmation before acting.
You favor whichever source seems most reliable in the moment.
You pick one of the two sources at random to save time.
You ignore both pieces of information and carry on regardless.

items.situation: The runway is reported contaminated (rain, slush) on arrival.

options.text: You land without a specific recalculation, trusting your experience.
You ignore the information about the runway condition.
You recalculate the landing performance before confirming feasibility.
You land normally while applying a general margin of caution.

items.situation: A difference of opinion emerges within the crew about the best way to handle a minor unexpected event.

options.text: You decide quickly based on your own opinion without discussion.
You facilitate a brief, rational exchange to converge on a shared decision.
You let the debate drag on without structuring it.
You avoid deciding and leave the unexpected event without a clear response.

items.situation: A significant delay could be avoided by slightly reducing a tolerated safety margin.

options.text: You refuse to reduce the safety margin despite the commercial pressure.
You slightly reduce the margin if it still seems acceptable to you.
You look for an alternative solution that doesn't compromise safety.
You systematically prioritize on-time performance over the safety margin.

items.situation: A sensor shows an outlying value that could be a false alarm.

options.text: You reset the system without prior analysis.
You cross-check with other indications before ruling on the sensor's reliability.
You ignore the value, assuming a sensor error.
You apply the procedure linked to that alert as a precaution.

items.situation: A strong crosswind makes the landing borderline relative to the aircraft's limits.

options.text: You attempt the landing while staying ready to go around if needed.
You attempt the landing without reassessing the limits on final approach.
You continue without paying particular attention to the wind parameter.
You precisely assess the limits and go around or divert if they are exceeded.

items.situation: You notice a minor anomaly during the pre-flight walkaround.

options.text: You decide on your own that it's not serious and depart without reporting it.
You don't mention it to anyone.
You report it and wait for resolution before departure if necessary.

options.text: You request a check but continue other tasks in parallel.
You have it checked immediately and wait for confirmation before proceeding.
You ignore the remark since it doesn't come from the flight deck.

options.text: You carry on as normal, they're minor mistakes in your view.
You try harder on your own without reporting it.
You pay no attention to it.

options.text: You deliberately conceal it to avoid any consequence for yourself.
You report it for review, even without a visible consequence.

itemScore.description: Each option has a rank from 1 (most appropriate) to 4 (least appropriate). Points for the chosen option = 5 - rank (rank1=4pts, rank2=3pts, rank3=2pts, rank4=1pt).

dimensionScore.description: For each dimension, sum the points earned on items 1-100 (control items excluded) belonging to that dimension, divide by (number of items in that dimension x 4).

overallScore.description: Sum of points earned across all 100 items, divided by 400 (100 items x 4 max points).

consistencyCheck.description: For each control item (id 101-110), compare the letter chosen to the letter chosen on the item with the same id as controlOf. Consistency score = matches / 10.

socialDesirabilityCheck.description: Share of answers (items 1-100) where the chosen option has rank == 1. Flag if outside 0.15-0.85 (over-optimized / atypical responding).

report.description: Narrative report generator: for each dimension, pick the band ('Low' if dimensionScore < 0.5, 'Mid' if <= 0.75, else 'High') and use report[code].bands[band] as the paragraph, plus the static strengths/suitableWork/tips lines. For the overall summary: if (max dimension score - min dimension score) < 0.2, use a 'homogeneous judgment' message; otherwise name the dimension with the max score as strongest and the one with the min score as the priority area to work on. Note: unlike SOSIE (a trait continuum), TD12 band thresholds are calibrated around the ~62.5% score expected from random guessing on a 4-option ranked item, so 'Low' here reflects a genuine below-chance judgment pattern rather than a personality pole.

bands.Low: Your answer choices depart fairly often from best practice in crew communication. This area is worth specific attention: in the tested situations, information flows better when a doubt is checked and shared immediately rather than deferred.

bands.Low: Facing uncertainty, your choices sometimes lean toward speed at the expense of analysis. Taking time for a methodical assessment, even a brief one, is an area for improvement here.

bands.High: You consistently identify the responses that proactively account for fatigue — a strength for human-factors management.

bands.Low: Your choices show a tendency to accept procedural deviations in some pressure contexts. This area is fundamental to safety and deserves particular attention.

bands.High: You consistently identify full procedure compliance as the appropriate response, even under time pressure — a solid strength.
